text: Johnson's praise of Shakespeare rests upon one principle, and that principle he gives without disguise: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature." (Johnson 1765). Those who wrote beside Shakespeare, as Johnson conceives them, drew men as some particular court or city had made them; their persons were adjusted to the fashions of a season, spoke the cant of a narrow circle, and were occupied with the follies of a single year. The season once gone, their force went with it. To the later reader there remains, in such figures, little beyond the outward habit of a vanished time. Shakespeare's persons, in Johnson's account, have another foundation. They act and speak from passions and principles which belong to every age and every country; a father's grief and a counsellor's vanity are not altered in substance by passing from Elsinore to London, or from the first spectators of the plays to those who come after them. Johnson does not suppose that the plays are without the marks of their own age; he supposes that these marks are on the surface, and that beneath them lies the common nature of mankind. Hence Polonius is credible to one who knows nothing of Elizabethan manners.
